docs.title: COMP 488 — Instructor Feedback and Development Plan
docs.text: Date: October 15, 2026 Project: AI-Assisted Cloud Monitoring & Troubleshooting Dashboard Context: Intermediate project presentation

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
This document summarizes feedback received during the intermediate project presentation and identifies possible improvements for the next development phase.

Some points are interpretations of the discussion and require further investigation rather than immediate implementation.

docs.title: 2. Container Management — OrbStack
docs.text: The instructor suggested exploring an alternative to Docker Desktop, possibly OrbStack.

docs.title: Action Items
docs.text:
• Investigate OrbStack and its Docker Compose compatibility.
  • Compare container management, resource usage, and ease of development.
  • Keep the existing Docker Compose environment operational.
  • Treat migration as optional.

docs.title: 3. Monitoring — Push vs. Pull
docs.text:
The instructor raised the issue of monitoring latency, particularly the delay between an application failure and its detection.

The current system uses Prometheus pull-based monitoring with a five-second scrape interval.

However, scrape intervals, alert evaluation intervals, and alert for durations all affect when an alert becomes available.

docs.title: Action Items
docs.text:
• Document pull-based monitoring and its limitations.
  • Investigate push-based or event-driven monitoring.
  • Explain why an application that crashes cannot reliably report its own failure.
  • Consider independent failure detection through container events or an external supervisor.
  • Compare detection latency and notification latency.
  • Implementation of an alternative monitoring approach is not required at this stage.

docs.title: 4. Timers, StopWatch, and Results Database
docs.text:
The instructor discussed timing measurements and a StopWatch example, possibly suggesting that experimental results could be stored for later comparison.

This interpretation requires confirmation.

docs.title: Potential Measurements
docs.text:
• Application failure detection latency.
  • Alert firing latency.
  • Incident API response time.
  • LLM analysis duration.
  • Container startup time.
  • Notification delivery latency, if notifications are implemented.

docs.title: Action Items
docs.text:
• Investigate StopWatch-style timing measurements.
  • Define repeatable experiments.
  • Record timestamps, durations, and execution status.
  • Evaluate storing results in CSV, SQLite, or PostgreSQL.
  • Compare results across repeated experiments.

Prometheus already provides time-series storage. A separate database should only be introduced if there is a clear requirement for structured experiment or incident records.

docs.title: 5. LLM Integration — Local vs. Hosted
docs.text: The instructor asked about the implications of using a locally hosted or externally hosted LLM.

docs.title: Action Items
docs.text:
• Compare local and hosted model deployment.
  • Evaluate computational requirements, latency, cost, and privacy.
  • Consider a provider-independent integration design.
  • Start with structured incident data rather than unrestricted raw logs.
  • Measure the response time of the selected approach.

docs.title: 6. Security and Log Protection
docs.text: The instructor emphasized the importance of protecting sensitive information when integrating an LLM.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Avoid exposing API keys, credentials, tokens, or personal information.
  • Minimize the amount of log data sent to external services.
  • Apply access controls to incident and log endpoints.
  • Treat application logs as untrusted input.
  • Consider prompt-injection risks.
  • Do not allow an LLM to execute troubleshooting commands automatically.
  • Review retention policies and access to stored incident data.

docs.title: 7. Lima — Removed from Required Scope
docs.text: The instructor clarified that Lima is not necessary for this project because related work has already been completed through the Cloudmesh AI VM project.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Remove Lima from required project milestones.
  • Continue using the existing Docker Compose environment.
  • Explore OrbStack separately.
  • Consider other cloud deployment environments only if time and project requirements justify them.

docs.title: Priority 1 — Documentation and Design
docs.text:
• Document monitoring latency and push-versus-pull trade-offs.
  • Compare local and hosted LLM security considerations.
  • Update the project roadmap to remove Lima.
  • Investigate OrbStack.

docs.title: Priority 2 — Experiments and Evaluation
docs.text:
• Validate Prometheus alert firing.
  • Measure failure detection and alert latency.
  • Record experimental results.
  • Determine whether a separate results database is useful.

docs.title: Priority 3 — Implementation
docs.text:
• Integrate an LLM for incident explanation.
  • Implement safeguards for sensitive incident data.
  • Test and evaluate explanation quality and latency.

docs.title: Optional Extensions
docs.text:
• Alternative container runtime.
  • Additional cloud deployment.
  • Persistent incident history.
  • Mobile interface.

docs.title: 9. Current Verified Progress
docs.text:
As of October 15, 2026:

  • Flask, Prometheus, and Grafana containers are running.
  • Prometheus is configured to scrape application metrics.
  • Grafana monitoring dashboard is implemented.
  • ApplicationDown and HighErrorRate alert rules are configured.
  • Incident API and rule-based troubleshooting are implemented.
  • Eight automated tests passed.
  • LLM-powered troubleshooting remains planned.
  • Controlled validation of alert firing remains to be completed.

docs.title: 10. Notes
docs.text: This document records instructor feedback and proposed follow-up work. It does not establish every exploratory suggestion as a mandatory project requirement.

docs.title: AI-Assisted Cloud Monitoring and Troubleshooting Dashboard
docs.text: Student: Khalidou Bass Course: COMP 488 – Cloud Computing, DevOps, and AI Instructor: Gregor von Laszewski Date: October 2026 Status: In Progress – Core Monitoring Implemented

docs.title: 1. Project Overview
docs.text:
The goal of this project is to develop an AI-Assisted Cloud Monitoring and Troubleshooting Dashboard that monitors a containerized web application, detects common operational issues, and uses artificial intelligence (AI) to explain possible causes and recommend troubleshooting actions.

The project combines cloud computing, DevOps, monitoring, containerization, automation, and AI into a practical system for understanding and responding to application incidents.

As an extension, the project will explore CloudOps Companion, a cross-platform mobile application developed using Flutter. This application will allow administrators to receive incident notifications, monitor application health, and access AI-assisted troubleshooting recommendations remotely.

The primary objective remains to build a reliable end-to-end cloud monitoring and troubleshooting prototype.

docs.title: 2. System Overview and Implementation
docs.text:
The system follows a phased implementation approach. The core monitoring pipeline is operational, while AI-assisted troubleshooting, cloud deployment, and mobile integration remain planned extensions:

  1. Application Deployment: Deploy a containerized Python/Flask web application locally and to selected cloud environments.
  2. Monitoring and Metrics Collection: Collect application performance metrics, availability information, and relevant operational data.
  3. Incident Detection: Detect selected incidents, including application outages, elevated HTTP error rates, and resource-related problems.
  4. AI-Assisted Analysis: Use an AI component to interpret monitoring information, explain possible causes, and recommend troubleshooting actions.
  5. Web Dashboard: Visualize application health, monitoring metrics, detected incidents, and troubleshooting information.
  6. Mobile Incident Monitoring: Extend the system through a Flutter mobile application for remote incident notifications and monitoring.
  7. Administrator-Approved Remediation (Optional): Explore secure, predefined corrective actions that administrators can explicitly approve.

docs.title: Target System Architecture
docs.text:
The target architecture consists of:

  • Application Layer: A containerized Flask application exposing health information and monitoring metrics.
  • Monitoring Layer: Prometheus for metrics collection and alert evaluation.
  • Visualization Layer: Grafana for monitoring dashboards and performance visualization.
  • AI Analysis Layer: An AI component for incident explanations and troubleshooting recommendations.
  • Backend API Layer: Flask-based REST APIs for providing incident information to client applications.
  • Mobile Layer: CloudOps Companion, a Flutter application for remote monitoring and notifications.
  • Cloud Infrastructure Layer: Local Docker deployment and selected cloud environments for deployment and evaluation.

The mobile application will communicate with the backend through authenticated APIs rather than accessing infrastructure management interfaces directly.

docs.title: 3. Technologies
docs.text:
The project is expected to use:

Technology Purpose Python / Flask Web application, backend services, and REST APIs Docker / Docker Compose Containerization and local service orchestration Chameleon Cloud / OpenStack Planned research-cloud deployment AWS Planned public-cloud deployment and comparison Prometheus Metrics collection, monitoring, and incident detection Grafana Monitoring dashboards and visualization LLM / AI Integration Incident analysis and troubleshooting recommendations Flutter / Dart Cross-platform mobile companion application Firebase Cloud Messaging Planned mobile push notification delivery GitHub / GitHub Actions / Makefile Version control, automation, testing, and deployment workflows

The final cloud deployment environments, AI integration, and mobile notification mechanism will be selected based on project requirements, available resources, and implementation feasibility.

docs.title: 4. Project Objectives
docs.text:
The main objectives are to:

  1. Develop and containerize a sample web application.
  2. Deploy and monitor the application locally and in selected cloud environments.
  3. Collect and visualize application health and performance metrics.
  4. Detect selected operational incidents using monitoring rules.
  5. Integrate AI to explain incidents and recommend troubleshooting actions.
  6. Evaluate monitoring behavior and compare selected deployment characteristics.
  7. Demonstrate an end-to-end monitoring and troubleshooting workflow.

docs.title: Extended Objectives
docs.text:
Subject to available development time:

  1. Develop a Flutter mobile companion application.
  2. Deliver incident notifications to administrators.
  3. Display application health, active alerts, and incident history on mobile devices.
  4. Present AI-generated troubleshooting recommendations through the mobile interface.
  5. Explore secure, administrator-approved corrective actions for selected incidents.

docs.title: 5. Expected Outcomes and Deliverables
docs.text: The expected outcome is a working prototype demonstrating how cloud monitoring and AI can work together to identify, analyze, and troubleshoot common application issues.

docs.title: Core Deliverables
docs.text:
• A functional containerized Flask application.
  • Local and selected cloud deployment configurations.
  • Prometheus-based metrics collection and alerting.
  • Grafana monitoring dashboards.
  • Detection and simulation of selected application incidents.
  • AI-generated incident explanations and troubleshooting recommendations.
  • Basic deployment and monitoring evaluation.
  • Source code, documentation, and a final project demonstration.

The primary workflow will be:

Application → Monitoring → Incident Detection → AI Analysis → Troubleshooting Recommendation

docs.title: Extended Deliverable: CloudOps Companion
docs.text:
The project will explore a Flutter-based mobile prototype with the following capabilities:

  • View monitored applications and their operational status.
  • Receive notifications when incidents are detected.
  • Review incident details and AI-assisted troubleshooting recommendations.
  • Access incident history and resolution status.

An advanced demonstration may include an authenticated administrator approving a predefined remediation action, such as restarting a stopped application service.

The mobile application will complement the web dashboard rather than replace it.

docs.title: 6. Project Scope
docs.text: The primary goal is to complete a reliable end-to-end prototype rather than develop a production-scale monitoring platform.

docs.title: Core Scope
docs.text:
The implementation will focus on:

  • Containerized application deployment.
  • Application and system monitoring.
  • Monitoring dashboards and visualizations.
  • Incident detection and alerting.
  • AI-assisted incident explanation.
  • Troubleshooting recommendations.
  • Basic automation, evaluation, and documentation.

docs.title: Extended Scope: CloudOps Companion
docs.text:
Subject to available development time, the Flutter mobile application will focus on:

  • Application and service status monitoring.
  • Incident notifications.
  • AI-generated incident explanations.
  • Troubleshooting recommendations.
  • Incident history and resolution tracking.

If time permits, the project may demonstrate administrator-approved remediation through a secure backend API.

Any remediation functionality will require authenticated access, explicitly permitted operations, administrator confirmation, and action logging.

AI-generated recommendations will not be executed automatically without appropriate authorization and safeguards.

Advanced features such as comprehensive cloud resource management, autonomous remediation, and production-scale incident orchestration are outside the initial scope.

docs.title: 7. Development Timeline
docs.text:
The project will be developed incrementally during the remainder of the semester.

Phase Activities Phase 1: Application Development Develop and containerize the Flask application Phase 2: Monitoring and Visualization Integrate Prometheus and Grafana Phase 3: Incident Detection Configure and test monitoring alerts Phase 4: AI-Assisted Troubleshooting Develop incident analysis and recommendation functionality Phase 5: Cloud Deployment and Evaluation Deploy to selected cloud environments and evaluate monitoring behavior Phase 6: Mobile Extension Develop a Flutter prototype for incident notifications and remote monitoring, subject to time Phase 7: Integration and Demonstration Complete testing, documentation, and the final demonstration

The core monitoring and AI-assisted troubleshooting functionality will take priority. The mobile extension will be developed incrementally without compromising the primary project objectives.

docs.title: 8. Conclusion
docs.text:
This project aims to demonstrate how cloud computing, DevOps monitoring, and AI-assisted troubleshooting can be integrated into a practical system for detecting and understanding application incidents.

By combining a containerized application, Prometheus, Grafana, cloud infrastructure, and AI-generated recommendations, the project will provide an end-to-end demonstration of application monitoring and incident response.

The planned CloudOps Companion extension will further explore how administrators can receive notifications and respond to operational issues remotely through a Flutter mobile application.

Together, these components will illustrate a practical approach to improving cloud application visibility, incident understanding, and operational responsiveness.

docs.title: 8. Monitoring and Alert Validation
docs.text: The monitoring system was tested locally using Docker Compose, Prometheus, and a containerized Flask application. Two controlled experiments validated incident detection and alert recovery.

docs.title: 8.1 Application Downtime
docs.text:
The Flask container was stopped while Prometheus and Grafana remained running.

  • Alert: ApplicationDown
  • Condition: up{job="flask-app"} == 0 for 15 seconds
  • Observed behavior: Prometheus reported the alert as pending, then firing.
  • Recovery: After restarting Flask, Prometheus cleared the alert.
  • Result: Detection and recovery verified.

docs.title: 8.2 High HTTP Error Rate
docs.text:
A temporary, loopback-restricted endpoint generated HTTP 500 responses inside the Flask container. Error simulation was enabled only for the experiment.

  • Alert: HighErrorRate
  • Condition: More than 5% HTTP 5xx responses over a one-minute rate window, sustained for 30 seconds
  • Requests generated: 481
  • HTTP 500 responses: 481
  • Test duration: 100.2 seconds
  • Observed Prometheus error ratio: Approximately 93.68%
  • Observed alert state: firing
  • Recovery: After restoring the normal container configuration, Prometheus reported no active alerts.
  • Result: Detection and recovery verified.

The simulation endpoint was confirmed to return HTTP 404 after the experiment, including for requests originating inside the container.

docs.title: 8.3 Automated Testing
docs.text: The project test suite completed successfully with 11 tests passed and no failures.

docs.title: 8.4 Alert Detection and Recovery Latency
docs.text:
Three controlled trials measured how quickly Prometheus detected application downtime and cleared the ApplicationDown alert after Flask restarted.

The experiment stopped the Flask container using Docker Compose, polled the Prometheus rules API every 0.5 seconds, and restarted the application after observing the alert in the firing state.

Prometheus was configured with a 5-second scrape interval, a 5-second evaluation interval, and a 15-second alert duration.

Metric Trial 1 Trial 2 Trial 3 Detection latency 26.171 s 24.147 s 23.657 s Recovery latency 9.795 s 9.275 s 9.787 s Detection from shutdown initiation 29.545 s 27.504 s 27.101 s

Across the three trials:

  • Mean detection latency: 24.658 seconds
  • Mean recovery latency: 9.619 seconds
  • Detection latency range: 23.657–26.171 seconds
  • Recovery latency range: 9.275–9.795 seconds

All three experiments completed successfully. Following the third trial, the Flask application returned HTTP 200, and Prometheus reported the alert as inactive and healthy.

These measurements represent client-observed alert transitions. Detection was measured from completion of the Docker stop command, while recovery was measured from completion of the Docker start command. They do not represent exact internal Prometheus event timestamps.

The experiment implementation, methodology, and results are documented in benchmarks/alert_latency/README.md.

docs.title: 8.5 Limitations and Next Steps
docs.text:
The experiments validate alert firing, resolution, and client-observed detection and recovery latency in the local environment. However, only three latency trials were conducted, and exact internal Prometheus transition times and notification delivery latency remain unmeasured.

API response times and workload performance have been evaluated separately in Section 9.

Future evaluation will include additional alert latency trials, cloud deployment comparisons, and secure LLM-assisted troubleshooting. The current troubleshooting implementation is rule-based; LLM integration remains planned.

docs.title: 9. Performance Evaluation
docs.text:
The containerized Flask application was benchmarked locally to evaluate HTTP response latency, throughput, and reliability under different workloads.

A reusable Python benchmarking script was developed to send sequential and concurrent requests to the /health endpoint and record response times.

docs.title: 9.1 Baseline and Concurrent Load Testing
docs.text:
Metric Sequential Baseline Concurrent Baseline Larger Load Requests 100 100 1,000 Concurrent workers 1 10 10 Successful requests 100 100 1,000 Failed requests 0 0 0 Average latency 3.35 ms 9.95 ms 7.47 ms P95 latency 5.29 ms 34.77 ms 10.28 ms Throughput 297.26 req/s 969.02 req/s 1,330.52 req/s

Concurrent requests increased observed throughput compared with the sequential baseline, although individual response times also increased.

docs.title: 9.2 Sustained Load Testing
docs.text:
A longer experiment repeatedly executed batches of 1,000 HTTP requests using 10 concurrent workers for approximately 31 seconds.

Metric Result Duration 31.00 seconds Total requests 29,000 Successful requests 29,000 Failed requests 0 Overall throughput 935.61 req/s Average latency 9.75 ms Median latency 7.88 ms P95 latency 17.61 ms P99 latency 26.67 ms Maximum latency 46.90 ms

All 29,000 requests completed successfully during the experiment.

The sustained throughput was lower than the throughput measured during the shorter 1,000-request experiment, demonstrating the importance of evaluating performance over different test durations.

docs.title: 9.3 Limitations and Future Evaluation
docs.text:
These results were obtained using the Flask development server in a local Docker Compose environment. The benchmark targeted a lightweight health-check endpoint rather than computationally intensive application functionality.

The sustained experiment used repeated short batches rather than one uninterrupted workload. Consequently, these measurements should not be interpreted as production capacity guarantees.

Future work will include longer continuous tests, resource utilization measurements, cloud deployment comparisons, and evaluation using a production WSGI server.

The reusable benchmarking script, detailed methodology, and complete results summary are documented in benchmarks/README.md.

By combining a containerized application, Prometheus, Grafana, cloud infrastructure, and AI-generated recommendations, the project will provide an end-to-end demonstration of application monitoring and incident response.
